objects.say: Both standards are down. At the head of the passage, bronze bars lift.^Up on the hill, two old men stop arguing for the first time in four centuries.| It does not last.

objects.text: {g}'HERE LIE USHUR AND BALTU, WHO KILLED EACH OTHER IN THE SAME BATTLE AT THE SAME MOMENT.'{/}^{g}'THE CITY COULD NOT AGREE WHO HAD WON, AND BURIED THEM TOGETHER.'{/}^Underneath, in two hands: {g}'I WON.'{/}| {g}'HE DID NOT.'{/}

{g}'EACH GENERAL TOOK AN ARMY OF CLAY INTO THE DARK. THEY WERE COUNTED, BY BOTH SIDES, TWICE.'{/}^{g}'THE WAY NORTH OPENS WHEN BOTH STANDARDS ARE DOWN. NEITHER WILL TAKE HIS DOWN FIRST.'{/}^Scratched below, by a mason: {g}'this is why we could not have two doors.'{/}

{g}'WEST: THE CAMP OF BALTU. HE WILL TELL YOU IT IS THE LARGER.'{/}^{g}'FURTHER IN, EAST: THE CAMP OF USHUR. HE WILL TELL YOU THE SAME.'{/}| Both camps are exactly the same size. The masons measured. They were made to.

{g}'THE BOARD. NO SPEARS, NO SLINGS, NO ADVICE FROM THE GALLERY.'{/}^{g}'A STANDARD THAT IS FLYING IS A GENERAL WHO IS STILL PLAYING.'{/}^{g}'RULE THE FOURTH: A PIECE THAT STANDS ON A ROSETTE CANNOT BE TAKEN.'{/}| Somebody has underlined the fourth rule. Twice, in two different hands.

A red drum and a blue drum, side by side, at the end of a passage that stops at a wall.^Nowhere else in the barrow do the two colours stand this close.| The masons were paid by the cubit. That is the kindest reason for a passage to nowhere.~~In the dream the wall is not there. There is a doorway, and beyond it somebody is being told, quietly, that he should have moved the other piece.
{g}'THE GALLERY. SEATING BY RANK. ADVICE BY NOBODY.'{/}^Under it, in two hands: {g}'HE STARTED IT.'{/}| {g}'I DID NOT.'{/}

{g}'THE GALLERY FACES THE WALL BY ORDER OF BOTH GENERALS.'{/}^{g}'IT IS THE ONLY ORDER THEY EVER SIGNED TOGETHER.'{/}| The board is on the other side of that wall. The gallery has been watching the wall for three hundred and ninety-one years, and every man in it has a view on how the game is going.

objects.say: The last of Ushur's spearmen goes to pieces.^The grille in front of his standard lifts. Nobody is left to mind.

objects.text: {g}'USHUR'S THIRD FOOT. MOTTO: FORWARD.'{/}^Underneath: {g}'THERE WAS A SECOND MOTTO. IT WAS ALSO FORWARD.'{/}

objects.say: The last of Baltu's slingers goes to pieces.^The grille across the ditch lifts.

objects.text: {g}'BALTU'S SLINGERS. MOTTO: FROM OVER THERE.'{/}^Underneath: {g}'A SLINGER FEARS TWO THINGS: A POLISHED SHIELD, AND HIS OWN AIM.'{/}

A bronze bowl on three legs, cold. The ash in it is older than the city wall.~~In the dream somebody has kept the fire in.^It burns blue, and the heat of it goes the wrong way: into the fire, not out.
{g}'THE GAME OF TWENTY SQUARES. RULE THE FOURTH: A PIECE THAT STANDS ON A ROSETTE CANNOT BE TAKEN.'{/}^Under it, in two hands: {g}'YES IT CAN.'{/}| {g}'NO IT CANNOT.'{/}| {g}'LOOK IT UP.'{/}

A sentry of clay, lying down. Every other soldier in the barrow was made standing up.^The potter had clearly met him.| He has his helmet over his eyes and his shield for a pillow, and he has not been disturbed since the funeral.~~In the dream the bench is exactly the same.^Nod is the one soldier here who looks the same asleep as awake. He practised.

{g}'NOD. QUARTERMASTER TO BOTH ARMIES, WHICH NEITHER GENERAL KNEW.'{/}^{g}'HE WAS THE BEST WE EVER HAD. HE WAS ALWAYS FINDING USEFUL THINGS IN HIS DREAMS.'{/}^{g}'THE ONLY PROBLEM WAS, WE ALWAYS CAUGHT HIM SLEEPING ON THE JOB.'{/}| It is the second thing they ever agreed on.

objects.say: It is over. It took three hundred and ninety-one years, and about nine seconds.^In the corner, a grille lifts.
The lamp that means the truce is over.^Along the wall, bronze lifts.| The truce held for three hundred and ninety-one years. It turns out it was the gate.

objects.text: {g}'THE TRUCE OF THE BARROW. NEITHER ARMY SHALL CROSS THE WALL WHILE THE LAMP IS COLD.'{/}^{g}'THE LAMP TAKES NO FIRE OF THIS WORLD. WE ARE NOT FOOLS.'{/}| Somebody has scratched under it: {g}'SPEAK FOR YOURSELF.'{/}
